1.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, What is the vine tree more than any tree, or than a branch which is among the trees of the forest? Shall wood be taken thereof to do any work? or will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel thereon? Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire devoureth both the ends of it, and the midst of it is burned. Is it meet for any work? Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less shall it be meet yet for any work, when the fire hath devoured it, and it is burned?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply the link that governs the chapter: the preceding word had destroyed the hope that a few righteous men might save the city, and this one destroys the other prop, the fancy that election itself put the nation beyond rejection, by denying that it holds any superiority over the nations at all.

Gill sets the parable among its predecessors, the siege drawn on a tile and the razor passed over the head, grants that the fruit is excellent while the timber is worthless, draws the moral that a people who owed everything to grace became on degenerating worse than any, runs through the trades that would have no use for the wood, reports that a Roman naturalist knew of curiosities made from vine wood though not of common articles, and presses the closing question that the unburnt branch would not have made so much as a peg before the flame ever touched it; Calvin describes the temper attacked, a people who boasted of a free kindness as though it proved them excellent by nature and used the gifts they were given as armour against the giver, and answers that whatever distinction they had was accidental and conferred rather than possessed.

Clarke states the chapter in a line, concedes that in some countries the vine stock grows thick while denying it is ever dense enough for furniture, insists the branch is what is meant and that he scarcely knows a more useless thing in any forest since nobody could make from it a peg for a mud wall, and turns the burning into a map, a branch catching at both ends while the middle scorches, so that the extremities of the country were already wasted while the capital stood under siege; Wesley puts it comparatively, that one branch off any forest tree is worth more than a whole vine except for what it bears, and says barrenness is what sends the wood to the fire.

Henry approaches the parable as a correction of the prophet's own likely thoughts about a noble city whose ruin was a pity, and answers that a fruitful vine is as valuable as any tree there is, once invited in the old fable to reign over the rest, its fruit gladdening God and man, so that a city planted as exactly such a choice vine would have been the glory of both had it borne fruit befitting a holy place.

debates.question: What exactly is worthless in the comparison?

positions.position: The wood as against the fruit: the fruit is excellent and the timber good for nothing.
Not the stock, which can grow thick, but the branch, than which nothing in any forest is more useless.
The whole tree measured against any forest tree, except for what it bears.

outliers.claim: Sets the chapter against the one before it, the first removing the hope that a few righteous men could save the city and this one removing the confidence of election itself.
Turns the burning branch into a map of the country, both ends alight while the middle scorches, the outlying regions already wasted and the capital under siege.

6.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; As the vine tree among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will set my face against them; they shall go out from one fire, and another fire shall devour them; and ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I set my face against them. And I will make the land desolate, because they have committed a trespass, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Gill describes a country left untilled with man and beast cut off; Calvin reads the burning as already half accomplished, the outlying country wasted and the northern kingdom cut off so that the capital stood like the middle of a faggot with both ends alight, is astonished that a people humbled by so many stages went on defying, disposes of two renderings of the branch by observing that a palm has no business among forest trees, explains that a city not reduced to dust kept a shape and a throne kept the people a name which fed the obstinacy, adds the folly of treating every reprieve as a deliverance until they laughed openly at God and the prophets, and takes the setting of the face for steady persistence rather than action in passing.

Clarke states the application as an equation of certainties, wood assigned to the fire and inhabitants assigned to be consumed, sums up the parable's purpose as bringing down the pride of men who in their best days had nothing but what was given them, takes the succession of fires practically, sword then famine then deportation with no escape on offer, reaches for the proverb about running onto one hazard while avoiding another, and calls the offence prevarication deserving the heaviest punishment while asking whether men suppose their darkest thoughts are hidden; Wesley finds in the wording an offending so unbroken that it reads as a single act.

outliers.claim: Explains the obstinacy by the survival of the city's form, since men not wholly consumed concluded they would not be consumed at all, and every lifting of the siege was treated as a deliverance.
Reads the succession of fires as sword, famine and deportation in turn, and quotes the proverb about running onto one hazard in the act of avoiding another.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; As the vine tree among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
And I will set my face against them; they shall go out from one fire, and another fire shall devour them; and ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I set my face against them.
